n10-licao-helm.enunciado:
Installing a real application usually takes several manifests (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap...). Helm packages it all into a chart, with the knobs you can turn in a values file:

helm repo add kube-learn https://pedromenuzzi.github.io/kube-learn/charts
helm show values kube-learn/loja            # what you can tweak
helm install loja kube-learn/loja --set replicaCount=3
helm list                                   # the releases in the namespace
  • Release: one installation of the chart, with a name (loja). Each change is a new revision.
  • Values: --set key=value or -f valores.yaml. helm get values loja shows what you chose.
  • helm upgrade loja kube-learn/loja --set image.tag=1.1: a new revision. Watch out: with new values, the upgrade starts from the chart’s defaults; to keep the previous ones, use --reuse-values.
  • helm rollback loja 1: goes back to revision 1 (and that becomes a new revision). helm history loja shows them all.
  • helm template: shows the manifests the chart would generate, without installing anything.

Helm stores each revision in a Secret in the namespace (sh.helm.release.v1.loja.v1...). Don’t delete those Secrets: without them, Helm forgets the release.
n10-licao-helm.vidaReal: The builder has a standard store design (the chart). You only pick the finishes (the values): how many clerks, which version, whether there’s a front desk facing the street. Each finished job is a release, with a history.
n10-licao-helm.limite: The standard design only lets you change what it planned for in the values: a finish the chart doesn’t know about is ignored, without warning.

n10-instalar.enunciado: From the terminal, add the kube-learn repository (https://pedromenuzzi.github.io/kube-learn/charts) and install the kube-learn/loja chart with the release name loja.
n10-instalar.dica: helm repo add kube-learn https://pedromenuzzi.github.io/kube-learn/charts and helm install loja kube-learn/loja
n10-instalar.vidaReal: Register the builder (the repository) and order the standard store design.
n10-instalar.limite: The repository is just the catalog: nothing gets installed until helm install.
n10-instalar.comoSaber: helm list shows the loja release as deployed, and the 2 pods come up.

n10-valores.enunciado: The valores.yaml asks for 3 clerks and version 1.1, but with names the chart doesn’t know. Look up the right names (helm show values kube-learn/loja), fix the file and install the loja release with it (-f valores.yaml).
n10-valores.dica: replicaCount: 3 and image: { tag: "1.1" }. Then: helm install loja kube-learn/loja -f valores.yaml
n10-valores.vidaReal: They asked for “three clerks and version 1.1” with the wrong names on the form: the builder delivered the default, without complaining.
n10-valores.limite: Helm doesn’t warn you about an unknown value: always check with helm show values (what exists) and helm get values (what was used).

n10-upgrade.titulo: Upgrade without losing what you already chose
n10-upgrade.enunciado: The loja release was installed with --set replicaCount=4. Upgrade it to version 1.1 (image.tag) keeping the 4 replicas.
n10-upgrade.dica: helm upgrade loja kube-learn/loja --reuse-values --set image.tag=1.1 (or repeat replicaCount=4).
n10-upgrade.vidaReal: The renovation only asks for the new version, but the job sheet was filled in from scratch: the 4 clerks that had been agreed on are gone.
n10-upgrade.limite: With no new values, the upgrade reuses the old ones; with any --set or -f, it starts from the chart’s defaults.
n10-upgrade.comoSaber: helm get values loja shows replicaCount 4 and tag 1.1; there are 4 pods on version 1.1.

n10-rollback.titulo: Bring back the job that worked
n10-rollback.enunciado: Revision 2 of the loja release swapped the image for a broken version. Using Helm (not kubectl), go back to the revision that worked.
n10-rollback.dica: helm history loja and helm rollback loja 1
n10-rollback.vidaReal: Yesterday’s renovation left the store crashing. The builder keeps the blueprints of every delivery: just ask for the previous one back.
n10-rollback.limite: A rollback is a new revision (3, same as 1): the history never goes backward, only forward.
n10-rollback.comoSaber: helm history loja shows revision 3, Rollback to 1, and the pods become ready again.

testes.descricao: the store is back on the good revision

n10-template.titulo: Look at the blueprint before building
n10-template.enunciado: Without installing anything, see what the kube-learn/loja chart would create with the Ingress turned on (--set ingress.enabled=true). How many objects does it create?
n10-template.dica: helm template loja kube-learn/loja --set ingress.enabled=true (each object starts with ---).
n10-template.vidaReal: Ask the builder for the printed blueprint, with the finishes you chose, before signing off on the job.
n10-template.limite: The template shows what would be created, but doesn’t check whether it fits in the cluster: quota, permissions and duplicate names only show up at install.

n10-licao-kustomize.titulo: The same blueprint in every city: Kustomize
n10-licao-kustomize.enunciado:
Kustomize already comes with kubectl. Instead of templates, it starts from plain YAML (the base) and applies tweaks listed in a kustomization.yaml:

base/
  kustomization.yaml   # resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml]
  deployment.yaml
  service.yaml
overlays/prod/
  kustomization.yaml   # resources: [../../base] + the production tweaks
  • namespace, namePrefix, labels: apply to every object.
  • replicas and images (newTag): the number of pods and the version, without a patch.
  • patches: a piece of YAML merged on top (e.g. resources only in production).
  • configMapGenerator: generates the ConfigMap with a hash suffix. Change the content and the name changes, so the Deployment that uses it gets updated: the pods are replaced on their own.
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod     # shows the result
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod      # applies it

In the editor, folders show up in the file name (overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml).
n10-licao-kustomize.vidaReal: The store’s blueprint is the same in every city; each branch just writes down its own tweaks (how many clerks, which version) on a separate sheet.
n10-licao-kustomize.limite: Kustomize only tweaks YAML that already exists: it has no logic (if, for each). For that, there’s Helm.

n10-kustomize-base.enunciado: The kustomization.yaml forgot the service.yaml. Add it to resources and put the label app.kubernetes.io/part-of: loja on every object (with labels).
n10-kustomize-base.vidaReal: The blueprint’s cover sheet lists the pages and the stamp that goes on all of them. Someone forgot a page and the stamp.
n10-kustomize-base.limite: Kustomize only reads what’s listed in resources: a file forgotten in the folder simply doesn’t exist for it.
n10-kustomize-base.comoSaber: kubectl kustomize . shows the Service, and both objects with the label.

testes.descricao: the complete base, with the stamp

n10-overlay-prod.enunciado: The overlays/prod overlay already puts everything in the prod namespace with the prod- prefix. Add to it: 3 replicas of the store (replicas) and the image at tag 1.1 (images), without touching the base.
n10-overlay-prod.dica: replicas: [{ name: loja, count: 3 }] and images: [{ name: kubelearn/loja, newTag: "1.1" }] (by the original name, without the prefix).
n10-overlay-prod.vidaReal: The big branch uses the same blueprint, with more clerks and the new version, written down on its own sheet.
n10-overlay-prod.limite: The overlay doesn’t change the base: the other branches (dev, staging) keep the original.
n10-overlay-prod.comoSaber: kubectl kustomize overlays/prod shows prod-loja with 3 replicas and image 1.1.

testes.descricao: the base is unchanged (1 replica, version 1.0)

n10-gerador.titulo: Change the color without calling anyone
n10-gerador.enunciado:
The store reads its color from a ConfigMap (COR=azul). Changing the ConfigMap to green and applying it doesn’t help: pods that are already running don’t reread their variables.

Replace configmap.yaml with a configMapGenerator with COR=verde in kustomization.yaml. The name gets a hash, the Deployment starts pointing to it, and the pods get replaced on their own.
n10-gerador.dica: configMapGenerator: [{ name: loja-config, literals: [COR=verde] }] and remove configmap.yaml from resources.
n10-gerador.vidaReal: Changing the notice on the board doesn’t change what the clerks already read. With a new board (another name), everyone is told they need to read it again.
n10-gerador.limite: The old ConfigMaps (with the old hash) are left behind: clean them up now and then, or use prune.
n10-gerador.comoSaber: After kubectl apply -k ., the new pods have COR=verde.

n10-licao-crd-gitops.titulo: New forms and the notary’s inspector
n10-licao-crd-gitops.enunciado:
CRD and operator

A CustomResourceDefinition teaches the API a new type: after it, kubectl get backups works just like get pods, with the fields validated by the CRD’s schema. But the CRD only stores. The one who acts is an operator: a program (in a Deployment) that watches those objects and does the work, creating CronJobs, StatefulSets or whatever it takes.

kubectl get crd
kubectl explain backup.spec       # the fields the CRD accepts
kubectl get backups               # the objects of the new type

GitOps

In GitOps, what counts is what’s in git: a controller (Argo CD, Flux) applies the repository to the cluster and, with self-heal, undoes any change made by hand. To change something, you change git:

git add loja.yaml
git commit -m "loja with 5 clerks"
git push

In this simulator, the inspector checks the repository every 30 seconds (and right after each push).
n10-licao-crd-gitops.vidaReal: The management office accepts a new form (“backup request”) and hires a specialist who knows how to handle that request. And the official blueprint is filed at the notary, with an inspector who sets the building straight on his own.
n10-licao-crd-gitops.limite: A form without a specialist does nothing: the CRD only teaches the API to store the request; the one who acts is the operator.

n10-crd.enunciado: The cluster has the backups.kube-learn.dev CRD and the backup operator running. Write the noturno (nightly) Backup: database loja, every day at 03:00 (0 3 * * *), keeping 3 copies. The file uses field names the CRD doesn’t know: look up the right ones with kubectl explain backup.spec.
n10-crd.vidaReal: The backup form has fields with specific names. Filled out in English, with other names, the management office sends it back unread.
n10-crd.limite: The management office checks the form (the schema), but not the content: a time that never comes is accepted all the same.
n10-crd.comoSaber: kubectl get backups shows the nightly one, and the operator creates the backup-noturno CronJob.

testes.descricao: the nightly backup, and the operator created the CronJob

msgs.2: the operator created the backup-noturno CronJob

n10-gitops.enunciado:
The store in this cluster is managed with GitOps: the loja.yaml in the editor is the repository. The manager wants 5 clerks. Try kubectl scale deployment loja --replicas=5, wait about 30 seconds (+30s) and watch the inspector put it back to 3.

Then do it the right way: change loja.yaml, commit and push.
n10-gitops.dica: replicas: 5 in loja.yaml, and in the terminal: git add loja.yaml, git commit -m "loja with 5 clerks", git push
n10-gitops.vidaReal: The building follows the blueprint filed at the notary. Changing a wall by hand doesn’t help: the inspector comes by and redoes it the way the blueprint says.
n10-gitops.limite: The inspector only fixes what the blueprint declares: what isn’t in git (an object created by hand) it doesn’t see.
n10-gitops.comoSaber: After the push, the inspector applies it and the store ends up with 5 pods (and stays that way, even after 30 seconds).
